title: Solution Story Architectures and Risk Mosaic — Sales Enablement
author: Maya López
body:
Purpose
-----
This page provides a concise, reproducible sales artifact that combines solution architecture patterns with an explicit risk mosaic (security, compliance, economics). It is intended for AE/SEs preparing tailored narratives for mid-market and enterprise prospects where procurement, platform engineering, and InfoSec are decision participants. Use this as a modular deck script and an on-call Q&A reference during technical conversations.

Quick summary (elevator):
- Problem: Teams struggle to run LLMs at production scale while keeping latency predictable, costs bounded, and security/compliance auditable.
- Redwood positioning: A single inference runtime and orchestration layer that delivers predictable latency, cost controls, and private deployment options (VPC / on-prem) with observability and fallbacks.
- Outcome for buyer: Reduce per-token cost by 25–60% vs self-hosted naive deployments with SLA-backed latency controls and documented audit trails.

Audience & usage
----------------
- Primary users: AEs and Sales Engineers building technical pitch decks for platform/product teams, InfoSec reviewers, and procurement.
- When to use: High-touch pilots, formal security reviews, executive economics briefings, and procurement evaluation cycles.
- Recommended format: 12–16 slide deck for execs + 4–8 appendix slides for engineering/security + one-page pricing scenarios.

Core messaging pillars (talking points)
-------------------------------------
1) Production economics: predictable unit costs + levers to control spend
   - Emphasize batching, KV cache, quantization profiles, and model routing as demonstrated knobs.
   - Callout: Redwood Optimize recommendations typically yield 25–40% token cost reduction for conversational workloads.
2) Deterministic latency & reliability
   - SLA options for Dedicated capacity, region routing, and automatic fallback to compatible model variants.
   - Observable, token-level latency breakdown available in Redwood Console.
3) Deployment flexibility & security
   - Hosted API for rapid proofs-of-concept; Dedicated pools for predictable throughput; Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) for regulated data.
   - Integrations: KMS/HSM support, SOC2-ready audit logging, and customizable retention policies.
4) Developer-first experience
   - SDKs, eval harness, and per-route analytics enable rapid iteration while preserving quality safeguards.

Competitive brief (summary of differentiation)
--------------------------------------------
- Large cloud provider endpoints: compete on scale and bundled infra; Redwood differentiates on inference-specific kernel optimizations, cost per token transparency, and unified rollouts across hosted/private modes.
- LLM API pure-plays: focus on simplicity; Redwood competes on production economics, predictable SLOs, and private deployments.
- Self-hosted stacks (open-source runtimes): lower sticker infra cost but high ops burden; Redwood removes operational lift with reserved capacity, autoscaling policies, and rollout tooling.

Buyer personas and tailored hooks
--------------------------------
- Platform Engineering (technical buyer)
  - Hook: predictable throughput, autoscaling policies, and programmable rollout controls; show runtime architecture and request routing.
  - Key questions: how KV cache is shared/isolated, cold-start characteristics, and rollback ability.

- InfoSec / Compliance (security buyer)
  - Hook: private deployment options, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logging, and data residency controls.
  - Key questions: network topology, credential lifecycle, and log retention / redaction capabilities.

- Procurement / Finance (economic buyer)
  - Hook: unit economics, committed discounted capacity, pilot-to-production cost predictability, and chargeback telemetry.
  - Key questions: overage policies, reserved capacity terms, and cost modeling templates.

Pricing scenarios (one-page guide)
---------------------------------
Use this table to orient prospects. Numbers below are illustrative; use official calculator for proposals.

| Scenario | Typical workload | Recommended plan | Pricing levers | Expected delta vs naive self-hosted |
|----------|------------------|------------------|----------------|------------------------------------|
| Pilot (small) | 200k tokens/day, low concurrency | Hosted API + caching | Prompt cache, small model | -10% unit cost |
| Growth | 1–3M tokens/day, bursty | Dedicated (shared) | Reserved capacity, batching | -25–40% unit cost |
| Regulated | 3–10M tokens/day, strict controls | Private (VPC) + Dedicated | Quantization + private runtime | -30–60% unit cost |

Pricing guidance bullets:
- Offer a 60-day pilot with consumption cap and clear success metrics.
- For Dedicated: standard three-tier commit (monthly, quarterly, annual) with clear overage rules.
- For Private: platform fee + implementation support; provide a TCO bridge showing reduced Ops FTE burden.

Pilot success criteria (example measurable metrics)
--------------------------------------------------
1) Latency: p95 request latency <= 500ms for 2k token responses in the target region.
2) Cost: measured tokens/unit cost within 20% of proposal model after Optimize recommendations.
3) Reliability: 99.5% availability during pilot window for production route.
4) Security: passed initial architecture review and filled SOC2/ISO questionnaire items.

Technical appendix: common architecture patterns
-----------------------------------------------
Pattern A — Hosted-first rapid POC
- Components: Redwood Hosted API -> Customer App; optional private data connectors.
- Pros: fastest time-to-value, no infra footprint.
- Cons: limited network isolation for regulated data.

Pattern B — Dedicated reserved capacity
- Components: Redwood Dedicated GPU pool (tenant-scoped) -> VPC peering for ingress -> Customer app.
- Pros: predictable throughput; soft isolation; SLA-backed latency.
- Cons: commit required for discounts.

Pattern C — Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Components: Customer VPC + Redwood Private control plane; optional on-prem inference nodes; KMS integration.
- Pros: full network isolation, auditability.
- Cons: implementation timeline 4–12 weeks depending on customer environment.

Security FAQ (concise answers to common prospect concerns)
---------------------------------------------------------
Q: Where do logs live and how long are they retained?
A: Audit logs are stored in the customer-dedicated log store for Private and Dedicated deployments by default; retention configurable per-account. Hosted API retains logs per policy and can be exported to customer SIEM via connector.

Q: Does Redwood support enterprise key management (bring-your-own-key)?
A: Yes. KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private and Dedicated deployments. Hosted API supports managed keys with optional customer-controlled rotations.

Q: How is PII handled during model evaluation and caching?
A: PII redaction and strict cache scoping are configurable. KV caches can be disabled or scoped per-customer; cached keys are encrypted at rest.

Q: What compliance evidence is available for procurement?
A: We provide SOC2 Type II report excerpts, penetration test summaries, and a compliance pack including data flow diagrams and retention matrices for Private deployments.

Q: What network controls support private deployments?
A: VPC peering, private endpoints, explicit IP allowlists, and optional on-prem air-gapped packaging.

Deal engineering cheat sheet (SE talking points)
------------------------------------------------
- If prospect cites a committed spend target, propose a staged reserved capacity agreement: pilot consumption cap -> 3-month ramp -> committed baseline.
- Use Optimize baseline to quantify expected savings and include token-level telemetry in the contract appendix.
- For security-conscious buyers, map each control to a deliverable artifact (e.g., KMS config, audit log export, architecture diagram).

Case study snapshot (short narrative to reuse in decks)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Customer: FintechPaymentsCo (mid-sized, regulated)
- Challenge: real-time fraud scoring with sub-second SLAs and zero-PHI leakage.
- Solution: Private deployment with reserved inference pools, strict KV cache scoping, and KMS integration for key lifecycle management.
- Outcome: 35% reduction in per-eval cost, 45% improvement in p95 latency compared to prior self-hosted stack, completed SOC2 questionnaire in 6 weeks.

Presentation playbook (how to run the deck live)
------------------------------------------------
1) Open with outcomes and economic framing (30–60 seconds).
2) Walk architecture patterns relevant to the prospect (2–4 mins).
3) Bring an engineering appendix for InfoSec questions and invite technical deep-dive only when asked.
4) Close with pilot proposal and suggested success metrics; leave time for procurement questions.

-------------
